cards.subject: math

objective.text: Solve word problems. Use a letter for the unknown number. Use Read, Draw, Write.

explanations.title: Read, Draw, Write
explanations.text: First read the problem. Then draw and label it. Last write an equation and a sentence that answers it.

explanations.title: A letter stands for the unknown
explanations.text: Use a letter like c or n for the number you do not know. Label it in your drawing.

explanations.title: Many equations can match one drawing
explanations.text: 7 plus 7 plus 4 plus 4 equals c works. 2 times 7 plus 2 times 4 equals p also works. 2 times the sum of 7 and 4 equals n works too.

examples.title: Hayride tickets
examples.text: Adult tickets cost $7 and child tickets cost $4. 2 adults and 2 children cost 14 plus 8, which is $22.

objective.text: Solve word problems in more than one way. Use a letter for the unknown. Explain your drawing.

explanations.title: Draw the problem two ways
explanations.text: Draw at least two ways to show the problem. Pick the one that shows it most clearly.

explanations.title: A two-step problem
explanations.text: Rain in two years was 282 cm. Year 1 was 185 cm. First find Year 2. Then find how many more fell in Year 1.

explanations.title: Make a friendly number
explanations.text: Think of 282 as 285. Then 285 minus 185 is 100. Take away the 3 you added to get 97.

examples.title: Rain in New York City
examples.text: 282 minus 185 equals 97 cm in Year 2. 185 minus 97 equals 88 cm more in Year 1.

objective.text: Solve word problems. Look at other solutions. Say what is good and what could be better.

explanations.title: Check a solution
explanations.text: Did the drawing show all the important facts? Are the labels clear? Does the sentence answer the question?

explanations.title: Pick an efficient way
explanations.text: Two ways can both be right. The faster, clearer one is more efficient. 24 times 2 is easier as 24 plus 24.

explanations.title: Compare with a friend's work
explanations.text: Explain how the other person solved it. Say how it is the same or different. Say what they did well.

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Group quadrilaterals by their attributes. Name trapezoids, parallelograms, rhombuses and squares.

explanations.title: Polygons and quadrilaterals
explanations.text: A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides and no gaps. A quadrilateral is a polygon with 4 sides and 4 angles.

explanations.title: Parallel sides
explanations.text: Parallel sides stay the same distance apart. They never cross, even if they go on forever. Think of the sides of the letter H.

explanations.title: Trapezoid and parallelogram
explanations.text: A trapezoid has at least one set of parallel sides. A parallelogram has two sets of parallel sides.

explanations.title: Right angles, rhombus and square
explanations.text: A right angle is a square corner. A rhombus has 4 equal sides. A square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles.

explanations.title: A diagonal makes two triangles
explanations.text: A diagonal is a line between opposite corners. It cuts every quadrilateral into two triangles.

examples.title: Fewer shapes with more attributes
examples.text: Each new attribute makes the group smaller. Only the most special shape, the square, fits the last group.

explanations.title: Quadrilaterals fit in nested groups
explanations.text: A square is a rectangle, a rhombus, a parallelogram, a trapezoid and a quadrilateral. Each group has more rules than the one around it.

explanations.text: A regular polygon has all equal sides and all equal angles. A square is a regular quadrilateral.

explanations.title: Same number of sides, same name
explanations.text: Polygons with the same number of sides have the same name. A six-sided polygon is a hexagon, even if it looks unusual.

explanations.title: Pick the most precise unit
explanations.text: To measure sides, use the smallest unit. A quarter inch is smaller than a half inch or an inch.

examples.title: A pentagon that is not regular

objective.text: Use tetrominoes to build rectangles and squares. Find their areas.

explanations.title: What is a tetromino
explanations.text: A tetromino is made of 4 squares. Each square shares a whole side with another square. Its area is 4 square units.

explanations.title: Turn and flip the pieces
explanations.text: You can rotate a tetromino or flip it over. This helps pieces fit together to make a shape.

explanations.title: Area as a sum of tetrominoes
explanations.text: Each tetromino has an area of 4 square units. A shape of 9 tetrominoes has an area of 9 times 4, which is 36.

explanations.title: Area as side times side
explanations.text: A square with sides of 6 units has an area of 6 times 6. That is 36 square units.

examples.title: A square of 36 square units
examples.text: 36 divided by 4 is 9 tetrominoes. The sides are 6 units. 9 times 4 equals 6 times 6 equals 36.

objective.text: Use tangram pieces to build new shapes. Compare their sizes and attributes.

explanations.title: Build shapes from pieces
explanations.text: Put two or more tangram pieces together with no gaps or overlaps. You can make rectangles, triangles, parallelograms and trapezoids.

explanations.title: Two small triangles
explanations.text: Two small triangles can make a square. They can also make a parallelogram or a new triangle.

explanations.title: Same pieces, same area
explanations.text: The square, the parallelogram and the new triangle use the same two small triangles. Their areas are equal.

explanations.title: Shapes share attributes
explanations.text: A trapezoid, a square and a parallelogram have 4 sides. Each has at least one set of parallel sides.

examples.title: Make a rectangle

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Learn that perimeter is the boundary of a shape. Tell perimeter apart from area.

explanations.title: Perimeter is the boundary
explanations.text: The boundary of a shape is its perimeter. Trace around the outside edge to show it.

explanations.title: Area is the space inside
explanations.text: The space inside a shape is its area. Perimeter is the edge. Area is the inside.

explanations.title: Cut and slide a piece
explanations.text: Cut a curvy path from a square and slide the piece to the other side. The perimeter gets longer. The area stays the same.

explanations.title: Measure perimeter with string
explanations.text: Wrap string once around the outside edge and mark the end. The marks compare perimeters.

examples.title: Trista's tangram square
examples.text: One side of the square is 4 inches. The area is 4 times 4, which is 16 square inches. The two large triangles are half, so 8 square inches.

explanations.title: Multiply to find the perimeter

cards.subject: math

objective.text: Build rectangles from a number of unit squares. Find their perimeters and see the pattern.

explanations.title: Factor pairs give rectangles
explanations.text: Each pair of factors of a number makes a rectangle with that area. 18 has the pairs 1 by 18, 2 by 9 and 3 by 6.

explanations.title: List factors in order
explanations.text: Start at 1. Ask: 1 times what equals the number? Then try 2, 3 and so on until you have all the pairs.

explanations.title: Same area, different perimeter
explanations.text: Rectangles with the same area can have different perimeters. The 1 by 18 rectangle has 38 units. The 2 by 9 has 22. The 3 by 6 has 18.

explanations.title: Long and skinny means greater perimeter
explanations.text: More sides of the unit squares are on the boundary in a long, skinny rectangle. A rectangle closer to a square has a smaller perimeter.

examples.title: Rectangles with area 18
examples.text: 1 by 18 has perimeter 38. 2 by 9 has perimeter 22. 3 by 6 has perimeter 18. Their areas are all 18 square units.

objective.text: Build rectangles that have a given perimeter. Find their side lengths and areas.

explanations.title: Perimeter is double the sum
explanations.text: The perimeter of a rectangle is double the sum of its width and length. P = 2 × (width + length).

explanations.title: Halve the perimeter
explanations.text: To find the sides, halve the perimeter. The result is the sum of the width and length. 12 halved is 6.

explanations.title: Find pairs that add to the half
explanations.text: List the pairs of numbers that add to the half. Each pair gives one rectangle. Turning a pair gives the same rectangle.

explanations.title: Another way: double each side
explanations.text: The perimeter is also double the width plus double the length. Double numbers until you reach the perimeter. Then halve each double.

explanations.title: Same perimeter, different areas
explanations.text: Rectangles with the same perimeter can have different areas.

examples.title: Rectangles with perimeter 12
examples.text: Perimeter 12 gives 1 by 5, 2 by 4 and 3 by 3 rectangles. Their areas are 5, 8 and 9 square units.

objective.text: Make a line plot of the rectangles found for each perimeter. Read it and find patterns.

explanations.title: Plot the perimeters
explanations.text: Label the number line with the perimeters. Use a ruler to space the marks evenly. Put one X for each rectangle.

explanations.title: Whole-number sides give an even perimeter
explanations.text: Add whole-number side lengths and double the sum. The perimeter is even.

explanations.title: An odd perimeter needs fractions
explanations.text: An 11-inch string makes a rectangle with a perimeter of 11 inches. That is odd. Its sides have fractions of inches.

explanations.title: Rectangle counts grow in pairs
explanations.text: Starting at 8, the number of rectangles grows for every other perimeter. The perimeters 4 and 6 match. So do 8 and 10.

explanations.title: More rectangles with fractions
explanations.text: Sides that are not whole numbers give more rectangles than the plot shows.

explanations.title: Area and perimeter plots differ
explanations.text: One line plot counts rectangles for a given area. The other counts rectangles for a given perimeter. We cannot make a general rule linking them.

objective.text: Solve word problems about perimeter. Use drawings, equations and statements.

explanations.title: Read, draw, write, check
explanations.text: Read and model the problem. Write an equation and a statement. Then check that the answer makes sense.

explanations.title: Regular polygon: divide
explanations.text: A regular polygon has equal sides. Divide the perimeter by the number of sides to find one side.

explanations.title: Two rectangles: add two perimeters
explanations.text: Find the perimeter of one rectangle. Then add to find the total for two rectangles.

explanations.title: Unknown side from the perimeter
explanations.text: Halve the perimeter. Then find the number that adds to the known side to make that half.

explanations.title: Perimeter is the length of the edge
explanations.text: The ribbon around a banner has the same length as the perimeter. Multiply it by the price per foot for the cost.

explanations.title: Check reasonableness
explanations.text: Reread the question. Check the units. Check that the answer is not too small or too big.

objective.text: Solve scaffolded word problems that mix area and perimeter. Use all four operations.

explanations.title: Three-step approach
explanations.text: Read and model. Write an equation, calculate and write a statement. Then check that the answer makes sense.

explanations.title: A square has equal sides
explanations.text: All the sides of a square are equal. The area is side times side. The perimeter is 4 times a side.

explanations.title: Joining squares
explanations.text: Three squares joined in a row make a long rectangle. The length stays 8 cm. The width becomes 3 times as long. Do not triple the perimeter.

explanations.title: Unknown side from the area
explanations.text: Divide the area by the known side. You can also solve an unknown factor problem.

explanations.title: Add all the areas
explanations.text: The wall holds three paintings. Add the area of Mason's painting to the other two.

explanations.title: Unknown side from the perimeter
explanations.text: Subtract the two known sides from the perimeter. Then divide what is left by 2.

explanations.title: Area not covered
explanations.text: Find the area of the room. Find the area of the rug. Subtract to find the area that is not covered.

objective.text: Solve multi-step word problems about area and perimeter. Use drawings, equations and statements.

explanations.title: Three-step approach
explanations.text: Read and model if it helps. Write an equation, calculate and write a statement. Then check that the answer makes sense.

explanations.title: Find the square's side
explanations.text: A square has equal sides. Think: what number times itself equals the area?

explanations.title: Leave an opening
explanations.text: A 3-foot opening takes 3 feet off one side. That side needs 4 feet of rope instead of 7. You can also find the perimeter and subtract 3.

explanations.title: Find the missing side
explanations.text: Halve the perimeter. Then subtract the known side to find the missing side.

explanations.title: Laps around a path
explanations.text: Find the perimeter for one lap. Half a lap is half of that. Use multiplication and addition for the total.

explanations.title: Only the outside matters
explanations.text: When shapes join, the shared sides are inside. Only the outside lengths count for the perimeter.

objective.text: Show one-half of a shape in different ways. Check that the parts are equal.

explanations.title: Equal parts matter
explanations.text: One-half needs equal parts. The parts must be the same size. The shaded and unshaded parts must be equal in number.

explanations.title: Estimate, then check
explanations.text: Looking is only an estimate. To be sure the parts are equal, measure or build the shape with unit squares.

explanations.title: One-half of a 6 by 6 square
explanations.text: A 6 by 6 square has 36 square units. One-half of it is 18 square units. Many different shadings can show 18.

explanations.title: Cut and flip a part
explanations.text: You can cut a piece off one side and flip it to the other side. The shaded area stays the same.

explanations.title: Half of a unit square
explanations.text: You can shade one-half of a unit square too. Cut it into two equal parts, and shade one.

objective.text: Show about one-half of a circle in different ways. Fold into fourths and eighths.

explanations.title: Fold a circle in half
explanations.text: Fold the circle in half. The fold line helps you show one-half. A ruler can help too.

explanations.title: Fold into fourths
explanations.text: Fold the circle in half, then in half again. Open it. The circle is divided into fourths. Color two fourths to show one-half.

explanations.title: Fold into eighths
explanations.text: Fold the fourths in half once more. The circle is divided into eighths. There are more ways to show one-half.

explanations.title: Get creative
explanations.text: Erase dots from the shaded part and redraw them on the unshaded part. Fourths that touch only at a corner also give one-half.

explanations.title: About one-half
explanations.text: We estimated with the circles. So we say the circles show about one-half, not exactly one-half.

examples.title: Folding steps
examples.text: One fold gives halves. Two folds give fourths. Three folds give eighths.

explanations.title: Rounding

Image models cannot count. Build every visual with exact counts by code, and have a person check each visual against its rubric.
All 1 assets are not_available yet: a_fluency_games. Items that use them cannot be launched until the assets exist.

visual_generation_rules: Diffusion cannot count reliably. Any picture where an exact number of objects matters must be built by code (SVG or widget) or drawn by an artist.

Every visual must be checked by a person: the count shown must equal the stimulus in the question and the rubric answer key.
Animations are described as frames with exact counts per frame, so they can be built or generated and then checked frame by frame.
Visual explanations are valid only when the asset exists (pipeline doc, Planner rules).
